A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LiveOIBench with the same 403-problem, 72-contest core benchmark. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and tables, figures, and mathematical content can be matched despite additions and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, inference-time scaling experiments, and reasoning-trace and error analyses in Sections 4–5 and Appendices D–E.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds model evaluations, language and prompt comparisons, contamination analyses, and manual validation studies.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction, offline code execution, and existing reasoning-annotation procedures are retained. Added validation studies and newly disclosed prompts and decoding settings do not establish a revision to the proposed method.

E1.justification: The original Olympiad corpus and task coverage remain unchanged. v2 adds a Python/Java/C++ comparison on 132 existing USACO problems and uses CodeContest solutions as an auxiliary reference corpus for contamination analysis (Appendices E.3 and E.7).

E2.justification: Grok-4-Fast-Reasoning and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 join the evaluated models in Table A9. Existing comparators remain, and the comparator membership in the algorithm-tag comparison, Table A10, is unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix A.1 replaces USACO Platinum's solved-problem medal rule with score-based thresholds. New protocols include a 22-contest language comparison, five prompt conditions, familiarity and code-similarity measurements, and sampled manual and cross-model validation. The retained best-of-eight protocol is unchanged; the PDFs do not establish that the medal-rule revision involved rerunning existing evaluations.

E4.justification: v2 adds several contamination diagnostics, language and prompt sensitivity studies, and model-size, reasoning-budget, and training-family comparisons derived from existing tag scores. It also adds audits of Markdown conversion, contestant-profile matching, and reasoning annotations, including a labeled error case (Appendices A.1, A.4, and E.3–E.9). Earlier scaling and temporal analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 introduces Pearson correlations with p-values, mean and standard deviation across five prompt conditions, and Krippendorff's alpha for cross-model annotation agreement. These substantially expand statistical reporting beyond v1. The prompt standard deviations describe variation across prompts, not repeated-seed uncertainty for the main leaderboard.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 retain their numerical results. Table A9 adds Grok-4-Fast-Reasoning and Claude-Sonnet-4.5, reporting pass rates of 50.95% and 27.05%, plus new division and difficulty breakdowns. New results include C++/Java/Python pass rates of 59.09%/56.82%/46.97% on the USACO subset, contamination correlations, prompt sensitivity, and 269 correctly classified annotations out of 313 audited events.

T1.justification: Section 5.4.2 newly defines document familiarity as the mean conditional probability assigned to its tokens. This is a limited quantitative-definition addition for the contamination study. The existing Codeforces rating equation is unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central benchmark contributions and conclusion that GPT-5 remains below top human contestants are retained. v2 updates the stated benchmarking scope from 32 to 34 models and adds an introductory claim of minimal correlation between performance, time, and task familiarity.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations linking low familiarity and solution similarity to limited memorization, and attributing C++'s advantage mainly to execution efficiency. It also discusses missed contestant matches, annotation and chunking errors, limited prompt coverage, and confounding in RL-versus-distillation comparisons. These considerably expand the earlier mechanism and limitation discussions.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly supplies the generation prompt, model-specific temperature and top-p settings, and additional token caps. v2 also documents template filtering and validation procedures, specifies a 3–6-month update cadence, and reports public resource availability where v1 promised release. Newly disclosed settings do not establish changes to retained experiments.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Claude Sonnet 4.5, Grok-4-Fast, Dolos, and CodeContests+, and connects its contamination methodology to the already-cited MLE-Bench. The related-work discussion and positioning against existing coding benchmarks otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained, with localized rewriting, terminology corrections, and an author-name expansion. v2 adds Sections 5.4–5.5 and reorganizes Appendix E around the additional studies, moving the existing reasoning-annotation material from E.3 to E.8.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 5, appendix Figures A4–A8 and A13, Tables A11–A13, and prompt boxes. Tables A7–A9 gain columns, and Tables A9–A10 move onto separate pages. The website screenshot is removed; existing diagnostic figures are retained and renumbered. These substantially expand and restructure the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important omissions in reproducibility and measurement validation: Appendix B supplies previously missing generation details, while Appendices A.1, A.4, and E.9 directly audit data preparation, human-profile matching, and reasoning labels. These additions substantially strengthen the paper's evidential basis. Some new contamination and language interpretations exceed what their proxy measurements establish, but those limitations do not outweigh the gains in transparency and validation.
